bib.title: STRUC-BENCH: Are Large Language Models Good at Generating Complex Structured Tabular Data?

question: How well do LLMs generate complex structured tables (raw text, HTML, LaTeX) from text, and can a structure-aware fine-tune of a small model close the gap?
hypothesis: Fine-tuning a small model on format instructions generated by FormatCoT lets it beat much larger LLMs on structured table generation.
contributions: We introduce STRUC-BENCH, a benchmark specifically constructed for generating structured tabular data.
We evaluate popular LLMs on STRUC-BENCH using two proposed metrics (P-Score, H-Score), giving insight into limitations and common error types.
We propose FORMATCOT to generate instruction tuning data (GPT-3.5 writes format instructions) and fine-tune LLaMA-7B to follow these formats.

method.summary: Benchmark of text-to-table generation in three formats built from RotoWire and The Stack. FormatCoT has GPT-3.5 describe the format of each target table; the description is appended to the input and LLaMA-7B is fine-tuned on it. Outputs are scored with classic metrics plus a GPT-3.5 judged P-Score and a heuristic H-Score.

datasets.name: STRUC-BENCH Table (RotoWire, reversed table-to-text)
datasets.source: RotoWire (Wiseman et al., 2017); tables larger than 3x3 selected; avg 7.26 rows & 8.75 columns
datasets.preprocessing: Descriptions checked on a review of 20 samples

datasets.name: STRUC-BENCH LaTeX
datasets.source: The Stack (Kocetkov et al., 2022) GitHub code; avg 2.75 rows & 4.47 columns
datasets.preprocessing: Table elements extracted; synthetic input descriptions generated by GPT-3.5; 50 tables sampled for quality check

datasets.name: STRUC-BENCH HTML
datasets.preprocessing: Same as LaTeX; manual interpretation template per format raised description satisfaction from 76% to 96%

other.note: Appendix A tables also list LLaMA2-7B, with no setup given

other.also: format-description generator for FormatCoT and judge for P-Score

training.objective: instruction tuning of LLaMA-7B on (original text + GPT-3.5 FormatCoT format instruction) -> target table

other.note: No fine-tuning hyperparameters, hardware or seeds are given anywhere in the text.

inference.samples: inferred: one generation per test item (no repeats stated)
inference.prompting: Instruction + input concatenated as model input; for raw text tables an example output is given first, then text and format description; HTML and LaTeX just specify format and content sections. First four models called via OpenAI or HuggingFace APIs without fine-tuning.

metrics.name: P-Score (content, format)
metrics.definition: GPT-3.5 scores content and structural similarity 0-10 after chain-of-thought; queried with predicted and reference in both orders and averaged

metrics.name: H-Score (content, format)
metrics.definition: Heuristic: format normalised via pylatexenc/beautifulsoup4/markdown parsing; average of Levenshtein similarity and difflib SequenceMatcher (Ratcliff/Obershelp); format score averages column-count match, row-count match, column-name similarity
metrics.unit: score (content up to 2.0, format up to 4.0 in Table 4)

eval.protocol: Automated metrics on test sets; human meta-evaluation by five undergraduates on 200 examples on a 10-point scale (instance-level Pearson); MTurk error analysis on 100 RotoWire outputs. No seeds, no significance test.

prompts.text: Describe details about the given text. First, give the number of tables, and then for each table, describe its format such as the number of columns and rows, column names, and row names.

Describe the format of this HTML in detail according to each HTML tag of the following HTML code. Be careful and make sure don’t miss any HTML tags. Please use more than 300 words to explain the format. Use specific numbers rather than being vague about several.

Describe the detailed format of a given latex table according to the commands and tags with more than 500 words. Include: Whether there are table border lines? How is text alignment? What are table attributes? Whether to bold? Whether to add \ref? Please clearly explain whether there are horizontal and vertical lines bordering each row and column. Say anything about a special "\" format token in latex if there is one. Don’t display latex code directly. Use natural language. And provide enough format information for me to recreate this table based on your output description.
Based on the example output above, generate the raw text/HTML/LaTeX table according to the following description.
Provide a description of the following tables.

Based on the above, we wanted to determine if the above tables are similar. Ideally, they should have identical content and structure. Score the "content similarity" and "structural similarity" between 0 and 10.

limits: No fine-tuning hyperparameters, hardware, decoding settings or seeds are stated; no variance or significance tests.
FormatCoT ablation (App F) is qualitative on one example (Fig 12, 13); no numeric ablation of FormatCoT versus plain descriptions.
The 'w.o.finetune' row is LLaMA-7B without fine-tuning, so it does not isolate FormatCoT from plain fine-tuning.
On HTML the 7B model does not beat GPT-4 on SacreBLEU and BERTScore; gains there are small.
Content H-Score correlates weakly with humans (0.1059).
Authors concede unexplored table format choice, domain-specific benchmarks, limited datasets, numerical reasoning, and multimodal.
GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 model versions and API dates are not given; P-Score judge is GPT-3.5, which may favour GPT-family style.

terms.definition: a self-instruct method in which GPT-3.5 describes the format elements of the output table, producing a format instruction added to the input
Prompting Score: GPT-3.5 scores content and format similarity with chain-of-thought, both table orders averaged
Heuristical Score: hand-crafted normalisation plus average of Levenshtein and Ratcliff/Obershelp similarity

problems: Table 2 and figure text extracted as one value per line; columns were mapped by order.

Appendix C.2 H-score formulas: Levenshtein similarity uses 1 - dist/(2*len(p)); Format H averages 4 terms (max 4.0), Content H averages 2 (max 1.0 by algorithm) yet Table 4 shows content up to 2.0, an inconsistency left unexplained.
